questions.problem:
The volumes of some chocolate muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $57\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $2\,\text{ml}.$
In contrast, the volumes of some pumpkin muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $42\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $1\,\text{ml},$ while the volumes of some blueberry muffins before cooking are normally distributed with a mean of $48\,\text{ml}$ and a standard deviation of $1.5\,\text{ml}.$
During cooking, it is known that chocolate muffins double in volume, while pumpkin and blueberry muffins triple in volume.

If a chocolate muffin, a  pumpkin muffin, and a blueberry muffin are randomly selected after cooking, what is the probability that the sum of their volumes is less than $400\,\text{ml}?$ You may assume that the volumes of the muffins are independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9842\,$ | $\,0.9846\,$ | $\,0.9850\,$ | $\,0.9854\,$ | $\,0.9857\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9878\,$ | $\,0.9881\,$ | $\,0.9884\,$ | $\,0.9887\,$ | $\,0.9890\,$ |
| $\,2.3\,$ | $\,0.9906\,$ | $\,0.9909\,$ | $\,0.9911\,$ | $\,0.9913\,$ | $\,0.9916\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{1}$, ${X}_{2},$ and ${X}_{3}$ denote the volume of the chocolate, the pumpkin, and the blueberry muffins, respectively. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(57,{2}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(42,{1}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(48,{1.5}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the total volume of the randomly selected chocolate, pumpkin, and blueberry muffins after cooking. Since the chocolate muffin doubled in volume, while the pumpkin and blueberry muffins tripled in volume during cooking, we have

$$
Y=2{X}_{1}+3{X}_{2}+3{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(2\cdot 57+3\cdot 42+3\cdot 48) \\  & =384 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={2}^{2}\cdot {2}^{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot {1.5}^{2} \\  & =4\cdot 4+9\cdot 1+9\cdot 2.25 \\  & =45.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y∼N(384,45.25).
$$

In order to find $P(Y<400),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<400) & =P(Z<\frac{400-384}{\sqrt{45.25}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<2.38) \\  & =Φ(2.38)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(2.38)≈0.9913.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>0) & ≈Φ(2.38) \\  & ≈0.9913.\end{aligned}
$$

A course grade is calculated by adding the results of a written test, oral test, and colloquium, contributing $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%,$ respectively to the final grade.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

$$
{X}_{1}∼N(64,{8}^{2}),\,{X}_{2}∼N(50,{10}^{2}),\,{X}_{3}∼N(60,{10}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the final grade of a randomly selected student. Since the written, oral, and colloquium contribute $50%$, $30%,$ and $20%$, respectively, to the final grade, we have

$$
Y=0.5{X}_{1}+0.3{X}_{2}+0.2{X}_{3}.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =0.5\cdot 64+0.3\cdot 50+0.2\cdot 60 \\  & =59, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & =(0.5)^{2}\cdot {8}^{2}+(0.3)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2}+(0.2)^{2}\cdot {10}^{2} \\  & =0.25\cdot 64+0.09\cdot 10+0.04\cdot 100 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ∼N(59,29).\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find $P(Y>70),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & =P(Z>\frac{70-59}{\sqrt{29}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>2.04) \\  & =1-P(Z<2.04) \\  & =1-Φ(2.04)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y>70) & ≈1-Φ(2.04) \\  & ≈1-0.9793 \\  & =0.0207.\end{aligned}

                    Finding the Distribution of a Sum of Normal Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that the random variables 

$$
X_1\sim N(-1,2^2), \qquad
X_2\sim  N(3, 3^2), \qquad 
X_3\sim N(4,2)
$$

are mutually independent, what is the distribution of $Y = X_1 + X_2 + X_3?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X_1, X_2,$ and $X_3$ are mutually independent random variables, where 

$$
X_1\sim N(\mu_1,\sigma^2_1),\qquad 
X_2\sim N(\mu_2,\sigma^2_2),\qquad
X_3\sim N(\mu_3,\sigma^2_3),
$$

then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2}+{\mu }_{3},\,{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
X_1\sim N(-1,2^2), \qquad
X_2\sim  N(3, 3^2), \qquad 
X_3\sim N(4,2),
$$

and

$$
Y = X_1 + X_2 + X_3.
$$

Since $X_1, X_2,$ and $X_3$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2}+{\mu }_{3} \\  & =-1+3+4 \\  & =6, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={2}^{2}+{3}^{2}+2 \\  & =4+9+2 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3} & ∼N(6,15).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

$$
X_1\sim N(\mu_1,\sigma^2_1), \qquad 
X_2\sim N(\mu_2,\sigma^2_2), \qquad
X_3\sim N(\mu_3,\sigma^2_3),
$$

and $a_1,a_2,a_3$ are real constants,  then 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y & ={a}_{1}{X}_{1}+{a}_{2}{X}_{2}+{a}_{3}{X}_{3} \\  & ∼N({a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3},\,{a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
X_1 \sim N(-1,3), \qquad 
X_2 \sim  N(3,2), \qquad 
X_3 \sim N(2,1),
$$

and

$$
Y = X_1 - 2X_2 - X_3.
$$

Since $X_1, X_2,$ and $X_3$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =-1-6-2 \\  & =-9, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot 3+(-2)^{2}\cdot 2+(-1)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =1\cdot 3+4\cdot 2+1\cdot 1 \\  & =3+8+1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}-2{X}_{2}-{X}_{3} & ∼N(-9,12).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A shop sells $2$ types of rice, Type $A$ and Type $B.$ The volume per packet for Type $A$ rice is normally distributed with a mean of $1$ liter and a variance of $0.01$ liters2, while the volume per packet for Type $B$ rice is normally distributed with a mean of $0.7$ liters and a variance of $0.02$ liters2. During cooking, it is known that Type $A$ rice quadruples in volume, while Type $B$ rice triples in volume.

If a single package of Type $A$ rice and $2$ packages of Type $B$ rice are randomly selected and cooked, what is the probability that the resulting rice volume is less than $8$ liters? You may assume that the volumes of rice in the packages are mutually independent. 

*Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\, 0.06 \,$ | $\, 0.07 \,$ | $\, 0.08 \,$ | $\, 0.09 \,$ |

| $\, -0.3 \,$ | $\, 0.3594 \,$ | $\, 0.3557 \,$ | $\, 0.3520 \,$ | $\, 0.3483 \,$ |
| $\, -0.2 \,$ | $\, 0.3974 \,$ | $\, 0.3936 \,$ | $\, 0.3897 \,$ | $\, 0.3859 \,$ |

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X_1$ denote the volume of the Type $A$ rice package, and let $X_2$ and $X_3$ denote the volumes of the Type $B$ rice packages. Then, we have

$$
X_1\sim N(1, 0.01), \qquad X_2\sim N(0.7, 0.02), \qquad X_3\sim N(0.7, 0.02).
$$

Let the random variable $Y$ denote the total resulting volume of rice after cooking. Since the Type $A$ rice quadruples in volume, while the type $B$ rice triples in volume, we have

$$
Y= 4X_1+3X_2 + 3X_3.
$$

The random variable $Y$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =(4\cdot 1+3\cdot 0.7+3\cdot 0.7) \\  & =8.2 \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={4}^{2}\cdot 0.01+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.02+{3}^{2}\cdot 0.02 \\  & =16\cdot 0.01+9\cdot 0.02+9\cdot 0.02 \\  & =0.52.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y \sim N(8.2, 0.52).
$$

In order to find $P(Y \lt 8),$ we convert $Y$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<8) & =P(Z<\frac{8-8.2}{\sqrt{0.52}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<-0.28) \\  & =Φ(-0.28)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
\Phi(-0.28)\approx 0.3897.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<8) & ≈Φ(-0.28) \\  & ≈0.3897.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When we form a random variable $Y$ from a sum of **mutually independent**, normally distributed random variables, the distribution of $Y$ is also normal.

More precisely, we have the following theorem:

*If $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ are mutually independent normal random variables such that*

$$
X_1 \sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2), \qquad X_2\sim (\mu_2,\sigma_2^2), \qquad \ldots, \quad X_n\sim(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2),
$$

 

*then the random variable* 

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+\ldots+X_n
$$

 

*is normally distributed, where*

$$
Y\sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2+\ldots+\mu_n, \: \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2+\ldots+\sigma_n^2).
$$

For example, if the random variables

$$
X_1\sim N({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}3}), \qquad X_2\sim  N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}4}), \qquad X_3\sim N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}1})
$$

are mutually independent, then 

$$
Y=X_1+X_2+X_3
$$

is normally distributed. 

Let's figure out the distribution of $Y.$ We start by computing its mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2}+{\mu }_{3} \\  & =2+1+1 \\  & =4, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & =3+4+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+{X}_{3} & ∼N(4,8).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It is vital that $X_1, X_2,\ldots X_n$ are *mutually independent*.

tutorials.problem:
When we form a random variable $Y$ from a linear combination of mutually independent, normally distributed random variables, the distribution of $Y$ is also normal.

More precisely, we have the following theorem:

*If $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ are mutually independent normal random variables such that*

$$
X_1 \sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2), \qquad X_2\sim (\mu_2,\sigma_2^2), \qquad \ldots, \quad X_n\sim(\mu_n,\sigma_n^2),
$$

 

*and $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ are real constants, then the linear combination* 

$$
Y=a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\ldots+a_nX_n
$$

 

*is normally distributed, where*

$$
Y\sim N(a_1\mu_1+a_2\mu_2+\ldots+a_n\mu_n, \: a_1^2\sigma_1^2+a_2^2\sigma_2^2+\ldots+a_n^2\sigma_n^2).
$$

For example, if the random variables

$$
X_1\sim N({\color{blue}2},{\color{red}3}), \qquad X_2\sim  N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}4}), \qquad X_3\sim N({\color{blue}1},{\color{red}1})
$$

are mutually independent, then 

$$
Y= \bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{3}X_1+\bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{2}X_2+\bbox[2pt,AntiqueWhite]{4}X_3
$$

is normally distributed. 

Let's figure out the distribution of $Y.$ We start by computing its mean and variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={a}_{1}{\mu }_{1}+{a}_{2}{\mu }_{2}+{a}_{3}{\mu }_{3} \\  & =3\cdot 2+2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1 \\  & =6+2+4 \\  & =12, \\ \text{Var}[Y] & ={a}_{1}^{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{a}_{2}^{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}+{a}_{3}^{2}{\sigma }_{3}^{2} \\  & ={3}^{2}\cdot 3+{2}^{2}\cdot 4+{4}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =9\cdot 3+4\cdot 4+16\cdot 1 \\  & =27+16+16 \\  & =59.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y=3{X}_{1}+2{X}_{2}+4{X}_{3} & ∼N(12,59).\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** It is vital that $X_1, X_2,\ldots X_n$ are *mutually independent*. If they are *not*, their linear combination may *not* be normally distributed!
